title: Repository

validation.research: Six authoritative source notes. Edward Hieatt and Rob Mee’s Repository entry in Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture establishes collection-like domain-object access between domain and mapping layers. Evans’s DDD Reference, printed page 17, supplies aggregate-root access guidance. Percival and Gregory explain small repository contracts, test implementations, and duck typing. Fowler’s Data Mapper entry establishes the representation-transfer distinction. Official SQLite and Python sources support targeted identity conflicts, parameterized queries, transaction ownership, and connection lifetime. The workshop contract, code, and native SVGs are original teaching material.
validation.python_examples: All three actual article fences execute as model.py, repositories.py, and demo.py with the five exact stated output lines. Both adapters pass the same contract checks for empty and missing results, immutable Workshop objects, exact-ID retrieval, inclusive seat filtering, deterministic ASCII ID ordering, case and whitespace preservation, quoted IDs, duplicate rejection without replacing existing state, invalid IDs/counts/object types, and domain capacity checks. Real storage tests verify old snapshots remain unchanged after a stored update, unrelated constraint and operational failures propagate, add does not commit, pending additions are invisible through another connection, caller rollback removes additions, caller commit makes them visible, and several additions roll back together. The caller retains connection ownership. Memory behavior is explicitly not claimed to model SQL transactions or concurrency.

Two workers, 20-second test timeout, and 60-second corpus hook timeout bound load on the large corpus.

example_limits: Python 3.10+ with SQLite 3.24+. The contract supports new additions, exact-ID retrieval, and one domain query over immutable Workshop snapshots. It deliberately supplies no update/removal API, dirty tracking, identity map, authorization, pagination, reservation, or concurrency protocol. IDs are nonblank ASCII text with exact case and whitespace; seat counts are whole units. The SQL caller owns commit/rollback and closing. The memory adapter does not implement rollback, durability, or database isolation. A returned capacity snapshot is not a booking guarantee, and a new read’s visibility depends on storage and surrounding transaction semantics. Arbitrary in-memory predicates are not automatically translated to SQL.
publication: Local implementation only. No publishing, deployment, push, or pull request.
